content: 1. The groups are divided into smaller factions, each with its own leadership structure. 2. Attendance at the VaRemba camp is restricted exclusively to members of the VaRemba tribe. 3. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) collaborated with the Ministry of Health and Child Care (MoHCC) to ensure the provision of safe, standardized medical male circumcisions (MCs) and to minimize adverse events (AEs) during traditional initiation rites. 4. The partnership emphasized cultural competency and sensitivity, with the long-term objective of scaling up voluntary medical male circumcision (VMMC) in the region. 5. After years of community sensitization, communication, and relationship-building, the VaRemba Camp Collaboration (VCC) was established to support the traditional VaRemba MC camp. 6. In 2016, two male VaRemba nurses were trained in VMMC procedures and the use of documentation tools for VMMC. 7. ZAZIC worked closely with a trained team of circumcised VaRemba men to promote the uptake of medical MCs. 8. In 2017, following a meeting with 14 VaRemba community leaders, the District Administrator, the National AIDS Council, ZAZIC, Mberengwa District Health officials, the Provincial Medical Director, and the National Male Circumcision Coordinator, the VaRemba formally adopted national VMMC guidelines. These guidelines included consent, counseling, and HIV testing as part of their initiation practices. 9. ZAZIC supported the mobilization of both VaRemba and non-VaRemba males in the area. 10. The camp operated from August 1 to September 6, 2017, offering VMMC to males aged 10 years and older, in accordance with MoHCC policy. 11. Of the 725 circumcisions performed during the camp, 657 (91%) were medical MCs. 12. Due to the support of VaRemba leaders and the approval of medical MCs performed by VaRemba nurses, nearly all eligible individuals opted for modern MC. 13. Since VaRemba nurses resided in the camp, all circumcisions, including traditional ones, were reviewed on days 2 and 7 post-procedure. 14. Only three cases of moderate infections occurred among medical MCs, all of which were promptly treated with antibiotics and healed without complications. Lessons Learned: 1. The VCC is one of the few successful initiatives in Zimbabwe that integrates traditional circumcision practices with modern medical MC. 2. The collaboration between ZAZIC, MoHCC, and VaRemba traditional leaders was the result of four years of consistent consultation and partnership, reflecting a shared commitment to the success of the VCC. 3. This partnership model, which respects traditional circumcisers and cultural practices, may be replicable in other Zimbabwean contexts and internationally. 4. In 2018, ZAZIC expanded its efforts to six other VaRemba communities in Zimbabwe, culminating in another successful camp collaboration in Gokwe South District, where 206 VMMCs were performed without complications. Additional Notes: WHO guidelines recommend VMMC for males aged 15 and above, with sufficient physical and cognitive maturity. Challenges in Manicaland Province (2018): 1. The three PEPFAR-supported districts initially struggled to engage age-eligible males (15–29 years) in VMMC, achieving only 40% of their targets in the first quarter of 2018. 2. Limited stakeholder coordination and involvement were identified as barriers. 3. Demand creation agents employed by an international NGO promoted VMMC without involving key stakeholders, such as the Ministry of Education and local leaders (traditional, religious, and political). Initiatives Taken: 1. Interpersonal communication agents used a segmentation tool to assess each potential client’s level of interest, enabling targeted and specific messaging. 2. Discussions with stakeholders revealed that VMMC implementers often operated in isolation or dictated program implementation, leading to resentment among stakeholders. 3. Meetings with provincial and district health leadership emphasized the need for genuine stakeholder involvement in the VMMC program. Results of Initiatives: 1. District Health Executives became actively involved in monthly VMMC planning, engaging community leaders and education authorities, conducting quality supervisory visits, and integrating VMMC with other health activities (e.g., HPV vaccination campaigns). 2. Enhanced collaboration between international NGOs and MoHCC improved service delivery. 3. Local clinicians were involved in service delivery, fostering local ownership of the program. 4. A dedicated team provided VMMC services at night (moonlight services) to accommodate sect members who avoided biomedical interventions, with follow-ups conducted by Apostolic clinicians from another province. 5. A WhatsApp platform was established for service delivery teams to share outputs, experiences, challenges, and ideas. 6. The international NGO introduced a District Field Officer to serve as a liaison among district stakeholders. 7. Engagement with schools improved, with over 450 teachers trained in VMMC mobilization in March 2018. 8. Community leaders, including political, religious (Muslim and Apostolic), and traditional leaders, were trained to deliver basic VMMC messaging and promote the program at public gatherings. 9. In areas practicing traditional MC, the international NGO and MoHCC partnered with these communities to have procedures conducted by trained clinicians. 10. From May 2018, the three districts began exceeding their monthly targets, achieving 102%, 138%, 123%, 134%, and 130% in May, June, July, August, and September, respectively. Lessons Learned: 1. Engaging and involving key stakeholders is critical for demand creation and effective delivery of VMMC services. 2. Coordinating all parties to ensure they fulfill their roles helps prevent program delays.
